title: Work Van Won't Start on Cold Saskatoon Mornings? Here's What to Check
body:
When Saskatoon temperatures drop below -20°C, work vans often refuse to start. This is one of the most common call-outs we get as mobile mechanics in Saskatoon during winter. Understanding what to check can save you time, get your van running faster, and prevent being stranded in the cold.

Start with the Battery
Cold weather dramatically reduces battery cranking power. A battery that struggles in summer temperatures may fail completely when it's -30°C outside. Check for corrosion on the battery terminals—white or green buildup prevents proper electrical connection. Clean terminals with a wire brush and tighten connections firmly. If your battery is more than four years old, consider testing it or replacing it before the coldest months arrive.

Examine the Engine Oil
Thick, cold oil creates significant resistance for the starter motor. Check your owner's manual for the recommended oil viscosity rating. Using 5W-30 instead of 10W-30 or 0W-20 can make a noticeable difference in cold-start performance. If you've been putting off an oil change and winter is approaching, now is the time to swap it out.

Test the Glow Plugs or Intake Air Heaters
Diesel vans particularly rely on glow plugs to warm the combustion chamber before starting. Faulty glow plugs cause hard starting, rough idling, or white smoke even after the engine warms up. On gasoline engines, check the intake air temperature sensor and consider having a diagnostic scan to identify electrical issues.

Inspect Fuel Lines and the Fuel Filter
Diesel fuel can gel in extreme cold, blocking fuel flow through the filter. If you run diesel, consider adding an anti-gel additive to the tank before cold snaps. Replace the fuel filter if it's been more than a year since the last change. For gasoline vans, a clogged fuel filter can prevent adequate fuel delivery during cold starts.

Check the Starter Motor
A weak or failing starter motor may crank slowly or not engage at all when temperatures drop. Listen carefully when you turn the key—a grinding noise or single click suggests the starter or solenoid may need replacement. This is especially likely if the van has high mileage or has had previous starting issues.

Examine the Alternator and Charging System
Even a good battery will fail if the alternator isn't keeping it charged. A faulty voltage regulator or damaged alternator belt can leave you with a dead battery despite recent replacement. Test the charging system or have it inspected during regular maintenance.

Look at the Coolant and Block Heater
Many work vans have engine block heaters installed specifically for cold climates. Verify the block heater is functioning by touching the engine block after it's been plugged in for a few hours. If the engine isn't warm, check the outlet, extension cord, and heater element. A functioning block heater makes a significant difference in Saskatoon winters.

When to Call a Mobile Mechanic
If you've checked these items and your van still won't start, it's time to contact a mobile mechanic. We can perform on-site diagnostics and often complete repairs at your job site or home, saving you the cost and hassle of a tow. Keep jumper cables, a flashlight, and an emergency blanket in your van during Saskatoon winters—just in case.

Regular winter maintenance is the best defence against cold-start failures. Scheduling a pre-winter inspection with a local mechanic helps identify problems before temperatures plummet and keeps your work van reliable when you need it most.
